newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico details U.S., IMF loan repayments.
newsitem.headline: Mexico details U.S., IMF loan repayments.

text.p: Mexico said Wednesday that it was financing the early repayment of emergency loans from the U.S. and the IMF mainly using money borrowed over recent months on international capital markets.
The Finance Ministry said in a statement giving details of the operation that the effect of the IMF repayment would be to increase the central bank's net reserves by $1.5 billion.
"It is important to note that the money destined for these payments is not coming from the international reserves of Banco de Mexico," the ministry said.
The ministry said the money to fund the repayments was raised from:
-- a $1 billion global 10-year bond
-- a $1 billion eight-year mark bond
-- a $650 million six-year samurai bond
-- $575 million obtained from the collateral freed by cancelling Brady bonds in past months
-- $550 million in debts paid by state oil company Pemex to the Mexican government
-- $500 million from medium-term notes issued by the government
The loan outstanding to the IMF is deducted from Mexico's gross reserves in figures given by the central bank.
The repayments were first announced live on television Wednesday by Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz in a ceremony at the presidential palace.
The ministry said that of the $12.5 billion drawn down by Mexico from the U.S. Treasury emergency loan, $700 million was repaid in October 1995.
Another $1.3 billion was repaid in January 1996 and in July Mexico announced the repayment of $7 billion more, leaving the $3.5 billion owing which is now to be repaid.
-- $330 million from a five-year lira issue
-- $395 million from "other operations by the federal government on international capital markets"

The ministry said the advantages of the early repayment were to eliminate the risk of refinancing public debt denominated in foreign currency, solve the problem of excessive short-term borrowing and improve and extend the repayment profile of the government debt still outstanding.

"This operation represents the conclusion of the process of refinancing of short-term debt denominated in foreign currency, whose amount at the end of 1994 rose to $41.4 billion and whose refinancing generated, in great part, the grave financial difficulties which our country faced at the start of 1995", the ministry said.
A large portion of that short-term debt was in "Tesobonos" -- Mexican government short-term borrowing denominated in dollars. All the Tesobonos have long since been paid off.

Finance ministry officials said Mexico still owed around $10.5 billion to the IMF after the latest repayment. They said they were negotiating a medium-term programme with the Washington-based organisation to soften the blow of repayments coming due over the rest of the decade.
((-- Michael Stott, Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9551))
